prompt: Which plant tissue carries most water from roots towards the leaves?
rationale: Xylem is the principal water-conducting tissue; phloem mainly transports sugars.

prompt: Which plant tissue transports sugars from a leaf to a growing root?
rationale: Phloem distributes sugars between sources and sinks; the other tissues do not perform this transport.

prompt: Which growing layer produces most of the new wood in a tree trunk?
rationale: Vascular cambium makes secondary xylem, or wood; cork cambium makes the outer protective tissues.

prompt: What are lenticels on a woody stem used for?
rationale: Lenticels provide openings for gases to pass through the bark, rather than producing pollen or seeds.

prompt: What carries sperm cells from a pollen grain towards an ovule?
rationale: The germinating pollen grain grows a tube that delivers sperm; the other structures have different roles.

prompt: After fertilisation, which part of a flower normally develops into the fruit?
rationale: The ovary becomes the fruit; anthers, stigmas and filaments do not normally form its body.

prompt: In flowering plants, double fertilisation normally leads to an embryo and what else?
rationale: One sperm forms the zygote; the second contributes to the endosperm, which nourishes the developing embryo.

prompt: What does it mean when a flowering plant species is dioecious?
answers: Male and female flowers occur on separate plants
Male and female flowers occur on the same plant
Every flower has both male and female parts
The species reproduces only without seeds
rationale: Dioecious flowering plants have separate male and female individuals; monoecious plants carry both flower sexes on one individual.

prompt: A mycorrhiza is a partnership between a plant root and what?
rationale: A mycorrhiza specifically involves a fungus and a root, rather than the other organisms listed.

prompt: Which organisms in many pea and bean root nodules fix nitrogen?
rationale: Rhizobial bacteria inhabit these nodules and fix nitrogen; none of the other groups is the nodule partner.

prompt: Biological nitrogen fixation first reduces atmospheric nitrogen gas to which compound?
rationale: Nitrogen fixation reduces nitrogen gas to ammonia; nitrate and nitrite arise in other nitrogen-cycle processes.

prompt: What carbon-rich food does a mycorrhizal fungus usually receive from its plant partner?
answers: Lignin released from living root cells
Carbon dioxide as its sole food
rationale: The plant supplies organic carbon, including sugars; fungi do not use carbon dioxide as their sole carbon source.

prompt: Which part of a seed embryo develops into the first root?
rationale: The radicle is the embryonic root; the plumule is the embryonic shoot.

prompt: What does the Casparian strip in a root help prevent?
answers: Water bypassing cell membranes on its way into the vascular tissue
Water entering the outer root hairs
Sugar entering any living root cell
New lateral roots growing through the root surface
rationale: This endodermal barrier blocks uncontrolled movement through cell walls, forcing water across selective membranes.

prompt: From which root tissue do lateral roots usually begin to grow?
rationale: Lateral roots originate in the pericycle, inside the root, rather than emerging from its surface tissues.

prompt: What is the main structural role of the large prop roots of a banyan?
answers: Attaching the canopy to neighbouring trees
Holding floating leaves on the water surface
Supporting flower heads above the foliage
rationale: Banyan prop roots descend to the ground and support the expanding tree canopy.

prompt: How does a compound leaf differ from a simple leaf?
answers: Its blade is divided into separate leaflets
Its blade has only a network of veins
It consists of several leaves on one branch
Its blade must have a smooth, unbroken edge
rationale: A compound leaf consists of distinct leaflets; a simple leaf has one blade, even when lobed.

prompt: A whorled leaf arrangement has how many leaves at a stem node?
rationale: Whorled leaves occur in groups of three or more; alternate and opposite arrangements have one and two.

prompt: What is a sessile leaf?
answers: A leaf attached without a stalk
A leaf made of several leaflets
A leaf that falls each autumn
rationale: Sessile leaves lack a petiole; the word does not describe leaflet number, seasonal loss or hairs.

prompt: In a pinnately compound leaf, how are the leaflets arranged?
answers: As separate leaves around the main stem
As overlapping scales enclosing a bud
rationale: Pinnate leaflets lie along the rachis; leaflets radiating from one point are palmate.

prompt: In a plant's xylem, what does adhesion describe?
answers: Attraction between water and the vessel walls
Movement of sugars through sieve tubes
Production of new water molecules in roots
rationale: Adhesion is attraction between water and another material, such as a xylem wall; cohesion is attraction between water molecules.

prompt: What mainly pulls water upwards through the xylem of a tall tree?
answers: Tension caused by water loss from leaves
Growth of the bark pushing upwards
rationale: Transpiration creates tension in the xylem water column; root pressure alone cannot supply a tall canopy.

prompt: What is an embolism in a plant's xylem?
answers: A gas blockage in a water-conducting vessel
A sugar-conducting cell in the bark
A new root growing from a stem
A waterproof band around the root cortex
rationale: A gas bubble can interrupt the continuous water column and obstruct xylem transport.

prompt: In which direction is the net movement of water between connected plant cells?
answers: Higher water potential to lower water potential
Lower water potential to higher water potential
Lower temperature to higher temperature only
Higher sugar concentration to lower sugar concentration always
rationale: The water-potential gradient determines net water movement; sugar alone does not describe all its components.

prompt: Which hormone made near a shoot tip helps maintain apical dominance?
rationale: Auxin from the shoot apex contributes to suppression of lateral bud growth; the other choices have different principal roles.

prompt: Which plant hormone group is named for its ability to stimulate cytokinesis, or cell division?
rationale: Cytokinins take their name from cytokinesis and promote cell division; the other hormone-group names do not.

prompt: Which hormones are used to lengthen grape bunch stalks and enlarge grapes?
rationale: Gibberellins stimulate elongation and fruit growth, helping produce larger, less tightly packed grapes.

prompt: Which plant hormone helps close stomata during drought?
rationale: Abscisic acid is a key drought signal that promotes stomatal closure and limits water loss.

prompt: Which enzyme attaches carbon dioxide to RuBP in the Calvin cycle?
rationale: Rubisco catalyses this carbon-fixation reaction; the distractors digest starch, fats or proteins.

prompt: Where inside a chloroplast does the Calvin cycle occur?
rationale: Calvin-cycle enzymes act in the stroma; light-driven proton accumulation occurs in the thylakoid lumen.

prompt: Which pair supplies energy and reducing power to the Calvin cycle?
rationale: ATP provides energy and NADPH provides reducing power; both are products of the light-dependent reactions.

prompt: In photosynthesis, what does carbon fixation mean?
answers: Incorporating carbon dioxide into organic molecules
rationale: Carbon fixation adds inorganic carbon to organic compounds; the other choices describe different processes.

prompt: Which mineral nutrient forms part of the phosphate groups in a plant's ATP?
rationale: ATP contains phosphate groups, which include phosphorus; the other listed elements are not their central atom.

prompt: Why are some essential plant nutrients called micronutrients?
answers: Plants need them in very small amounts
They are optional for healthy growth
They are all smaller atoms than other nutrients
rationale: Micronutrients are defined by the small quantities required, not by their importance or atomic size.

prompt: What distinguishes hydroponic plant growing from ordinary soil cultivation?
answers: Nutrients are supplied in a water-based solution without soil
Plants receive nutrients only through dry soil
Plants are grown entirely from leaf cuttings
Plants are trained into miniature tree shapes
rationale: Hydroponics replaces soil with a nutrient solution; suitable water, minerals and light are still needed.

prompt: Which term describes abnormal yellowing of leaves caused by loss of chlorophyll?
rationale: Chlorosis is chlorophyll-related yellowing; necrosis is tissue death, abscission is shedding and lignification is wall hardening.

prompt: Which soil component comes mainly from the decomposition of organic material?
rationale: Humus is organic material derived from decay; the other choices are mineral components.

prompt: What is a distinct layer in a soil profile called?
rationale: A horizon is a distinct soil layer; aggregates, pores and grains are smaller structural components.

prompt: Among these soil particles, which are the smallest?
rationale: Clay particles are smaller than silt, sand and gravel under standard soil size classifications.

prompt: What is the rhizosphere?
answers: The soil region influenced by living roots
The outer surface of a flower
The hollow centre of a stem
The seed coat surrounding an embryo
rationale: The rhizosphere is the root-influenced soil zone, where root secretions affect microorganisms.

prompt: What does scarification do to a seed before sowing?
answers: Weakens or breaks its hard outer coat
Chills it in a moist medium
Gradually exposes seedlings to outdoor conditions
rationale: Scarification allows water and gases through a resistant seed coat without deliberately destroying the embryo.

prompt: What does cold stratification involve?
answers: Keeping seeds moist and cold for a period
Scratching the seed coat with an abrasive
Gradually increasing light on young seedlings
rationale: Cold, moist treatment can satisfy a seed's chilling requirement and help release dormancy.

prompt: Why can waterlogged seed compost prevent germination?
answers: It restricts the oxygen available for respiration
It always keeps the seed too warm
It prevents seeds from absorbing water
It permanently hardens every seed coat
rationale: Germinating seeds respire; saturated pore spaces limit oxygen, whereas the other proposed effects are incorrect.

prompt: For seeds that need light to germinate, which sowing method is most appropriate?
answers: Sowing on or very near the surface
Burying under several centimetres of soil
Wrapping in opaque foil after sowing
Covering with a thick bark mulch
rationale: Light-requiring seeds must receive light; deep soil, foil and thick mulch block it.

prompt: What describes the stem used for a semi-ripe cutting?
answers: Firm at the base but still soft at the tip
A piece of root without any stem
A leaf detached without a stalk
rationale: Semi-ripe material has partly matured; its base is firm while its tip remains softer.

prompt: What is the heel on a heel cutting?
answers: A small piece of older stem attached at its base
rationale: A heel cutting retains older stem tissue where the shoot was pulled away; it is not a root or treatment.

prompt: Why are large leaves sometimes cut in half when preparing leafy cuttings?
answers: To reduce water loss before roots develop
To increase the total leaf area
To remove all stored food from the cutting
To prevent the stem forming any new roots
rationale: Reducing leaf area lowers transpiration while the cutting has limited ability to replace lost water.

prompt: When are hardwood cuttings of deciduous shrubs generally taken in the UK?
answers: During dormancy, from autumn to late winter
During the first flush of soft spring growth
At the height of midsummer flowering
Only after the shrub has started new autumn shoots
rationale: Hardwood cuttings use mature growth during the dormant season, usually after leaf fall.

prompt: In grafting, what is the scion?
answers: The shoot or bud of the chosen variety
rationale: The scion provides the desired upper growth; the root system belongs to the rootstock.

prompt: Which layers must make good contact when a tree is grafted?
rationale: Cambial contact allows the graft partners to join and develop a vascular connection.

prompt: Why are apple varieties often grafted onto dwarfing rootstocks?
answers: To limit the eventual size of the tree
To eliminate the need for sunlight
rationale: A dwarfing rootstock restricts vigour and tree size while retaining the chosen apple variety above the graft.

prompt: What does F1 mean on a packet of hybrid seeds?
answers: The first generation from the parental cross
The first plant to flower each year
A plant that survives one frost
rationale: F1 identifies the first filial generation, not flowering order, seed-leaf number or hardiness.

prompt: Why might seed saved from an F1 hybrid produce noticeably varied plants?
answers: Genetic combinations separate and recombine in the offspring
The seed coats all mutate into a new species
Every seed loses the genes inherited from one parent
The seedlings are exact clones of different neighbours
rationale: Sexual reproduction reshuffles the hybrid's inherited genetic combinations, so its offspring need not match the parent.

prompt: What is another name for hybrid vigour?
rationale: Heterosis means enhanced performance in a hybrid; chlorosis is yellowing and abscission is shedding.

prompt: Which generation is produced when F1 hybrid plants are self-pollinated?
rationale: Their sexually produced offspring form the F2 generation, rather than remaining F1 or becoming clones.

prompt: If an established Group 1 clematis needs pruning, when is the usual time?
answers: After its spring flowers have finished
Just before its spring flowers open
Before every leaf has fallen in autumn
rationale: Group 1 flowers on previous-season growth; pruning after flowering preserves the current display.

prompt: On which growth do Group 3 clematis produce their summer flowers?
answers: Only shoots produced two years earlier
rationale: Group 3 clematis flower on new growth, so hard late-winter pruning does not remove the coming summer's flowers.

prompt: In UK gardening, which clematis pruning group includes many large-flowered varieties that bloom in early summer and may repeat later?
rationale: Group 2 includes these repeat-flowering large-flowered cultivars; the standard clematis system has three groups.

prompt: Coir used in potting compost comes from which material?
rationale: Coir is coconut-husk fibre; the other materials are not its source.

prompt: Which potting-compost ingredient is made by expanding volcanic rock with heat?
rationale: Heated volcanic rock expands into porous perlite; the other choices are plant-derived materials.

prompt: Which compost ingredient consists of light, silvery-brown mineral flakes that hold moisture?
rationale: Vermiculite is a water-absorbing mineral; coir and bark are organic, and sand is not flaky or spongy.

prompt: Why does avoiding peat extraction help protect the climate?
answers: Peatlands store carbon that disturbance can release
Drained peat always absorbs more carbon than intact peat
Extracted peat permanently removes carbon from circulation
rationale: Damaging and draining peatlands can release stored carbon; preserving them protects that store.

prompt: Epsom salts can supply which nutrient to a plant with a confirmed deficiency?
rationale: Epsom salts are magnesium sulphate, so they supply magnesium rather than the other listed nutrients.

prompt: Why can an acid-loving plant develop iron deficiency in chalky soil?
answers: High pH makes iron harder for its roots to take up
High pH makes iron unnecessary for chlorophyll formation
Chalk supplies nitrogen in place of every trace element
Chalk prevents all water from entering the plant
rationale: Alkaline conditions reduce iron availability even when soil contains iron.

prompt: Blossom-end rot in tomatoes is associated with inadequate delivery of which nutrient to the fruit?
rationale: Insufficient calcium reaching developing fruit causes the disorder, often because water supply is uneven.

prompt: Which disease commonly coats plant leaves with a white, dusty fungal growth?
rationale: Powdery mildew forms superficial white growth; the other diseases do not characteristically produce this coating.

prompt: What produces the coloured spore pustules of a plant rust disease?
rationale: Rusts are fungal diseases; their pustules contain fungal spores.

prompt: Rose black spot often causes affected leaves to do what?
answers: Stay green for an extra growing season
Develop a stronger wax layer without damage
rationale: Black spot damages foliage and can cause yellowing and premature leaf fall, reducing photosynthetic capacity.

prompt: Which tree is recognisable by its fan-shaped leaves, often divided into two lobes?
rationale: Ginkgo has distinctive fan-shaped leaves; the other listed trees have differently shaped blades.

prompt: Ginkgo trees are native to which country?
rationale: Surviving native ginkgo populations are in China; cultivation elsewhere does not make those regions native.

prompt: Ginkgo belongs to which major group of seed plants?
rationale: Ginkgo is a gymnosperm; it produces seeds without flowers, unlike angiosperms.

prompt: Which part of a cork oak is harvested to make natural bottle stoppers?
rationale: Commercial cork is harvested bark; the other organs do not supply it.

prompt: The cork oak is native to which region?
rationale: The native range lies around the western and central Mediterranean, including southern Europe and northern Africa.

prompt: Why can a cork oak be harvested repeatedly without being felled?
answers: It regenerates the carefully removed cork layer
The harvested cork comes from dead branches only
The whole trunk is replaced each year
Harvesting removes only loose autumn leaves
rationale: Skilled cork stripping preserves living tissues, allowing a fresh cork layer to form.

prompt: The backward-pointing extensions on many columbine petals are called what?
rationale: Columbine petals have spurs; the other structures are not petal extensions.

prompt: Which garden flower is also known as granny's bonnet?
rationale: Granny's bonnet is a common name for columbine, or Aquilegia.

prompt: Which perennial bears rows of hanging, heart-shaped flowers on arching stems?
rationale: Bleeding heart has this characteristic pendant flower shape; the distractors have differently arranged flowers.

prompt: Which spring flower is known for its nodding purple bells with a chequered pattern?
rationale: Snake's head fritillary has chequered bell-shaped flowers; the other choices lack this characteristic pattern.

prompt: How are the leaves typically arranged along a dawn redwood's short shoots?
answers: In rings of three scale leaves
rationale: Dawn redwood foliage is arranged in opposite or nearly opposite pairs along the shoots, unlike the other patterns listed.

prompt: Living dawn redwoods were identified in China in the 1940s after the tree was known from what?
answers: A surviving collection of Roman seedlings
rationale: The genus was known from fossil material before living trees were recognised in China.

prompt: Which plant produces a single giant flower rather than a head containing many tiny flowers?
rationale: Rafflesia produces an individual flower; the other spectacular displays are inflorescences.

prompt: How does the leafless Rafflesia obtain nourishment?
answers: By living as a parasite inside a host vine
By catching insects in its flower
By absorbing minerals through its own large roots
rationale: Rafflesia lives within Tetrastigma vines and lacks ordinary roots and leaves; it is not carnivorous.

prompt: Which small succulents are commonly called living stones?
rationale: Lithops have pebble-like bodies; the other listed succulents typically form conspicuous leaf rosettes.

prompt: What is the purpose of translucent windows on Lithops leaves?
answers: Letting light reach photosynthetic tissue within the plant
Allowing insects to enter a trap
rationale: The windows transmit light into leaves that are partly underground; they are not reproductive or trapping structures.

prompt: What triggers the seed capsules of many Lithops to open?
rationale: These capsules open when wet, making their small seeds available for rain-assisted dispersal.

prompt: What do the upward-growing pneumatophores of black mangroves provide?
answers: Access to oxygen for buried roots
Sites where the tree forms its seeds
Anchors that attach branches to nearby trees
rationale: Pneumatophores connect oxygen-poor buried tissues with air; their main role is gas exchange.

prompt: How do red mangroves keep much of the surrounding salt out of their tissues?
answers: By filtering it at their roots
By converting sodium chloride into sugar
By absorbing seawater only through flowers
By using salt in place of chlorophyll
rationale: Root membranes exclude much of the salt while allowing water uptake; the other mechanisms are incorrect.

prompt: In mangroves, what does vivipary mean?
answers: Seeds germinate while still attached to the parent
New plants grow only from detached leaves
Pollen fertilises a flower on the same plant
Seeds stay dormant until the parent dies
rationale: Vivipary describes germination before a propagule leaves the parent, rather than a root or leaf behaviour.

prompt: Unlike seaweeds, seagrasses belong to which plant group?
rationale: Seagrasses have roots, flowers and seeds; seaweeds are algae.

prompt: Why are seagrass meadows usually found in relatively shallow water?
answers: Enough sunlight must reach them for photosynthesis
They require fresh water rather than seawater
Their flowers must remain above the surface
Their roots can absorb nutrients only from air
rationale: Light limits the depths at which seagrasses can photosynthesise; the other choices misdescribe marine plants.

prompt: What can carry pollen between seagrass flowers underwater?
answers: Dry air flowing between the flowers
Pollen tubes growing through the seabed
rationale: Water movement transports seagrass pollen; some species also receive help from small marine animals.

prompt: What happens to water droplets on a healthy sacred lotus leaf?
answers: They bead up and roll off
They spread into a continuous film
They soak through the blade like blotting paper
They become trapped in absorbent leaf hairs
rationale: The highly water-repellent surface makes droplets bead and roll away.

prompt: Which surface feature helps lotus leaves repel water so effectively?
answers: Tiny bumps coated in waxy structures
Large open holes through the blade
A permanent layer of loose pollen
A covering of exposed root hairs
rationale: Microscopic texture and wax reduce water contact; the other features do not create the lotus effect.

prompt: Sacred lotus flowers can attract insects partly by regulating what?
answers: The salt concentration of the whole pond
The direction of nearby water currents
rationale: Sacred lotus flowers generate heat and regulate temperature; the other environmental and genetic changes are not their mechanism.

prompt: Which familiar food plant belongs to the bromeliad family?
rationale: Bromeliaceae is the pineapple family; the other fruit plants belong to different families.

prompt: Where do tank bromeliads collect rainwater?
rationale: Overlapping leaf bases form water-holding spaces; underground tubers, seed capsules and loose bark are not the tank.

prompt: Which specialised leaf structures help air-plant bromeliads absorb water?
rationale: Specialised trichomes absorb moisture and minerals; the distractors are not these leaf-surface structures.

prompt: How does an epiphytic bromeliad use the tree on which it grows?
answers: As a support, without feeding parasitically on it
As a source of sap tapped through feeding roots
As a source of pollen for every flower
As a replacement for its own chlorophyll
rationale: An epiphyte uses its host for support while obtaining resources independently; it is not a sap-feeding parasite.

prompt: An agave described as monocarpic does what?
answers: Flowers in one reproductive episode and then dies
Produces exactly one individual flower each year
Makes male flowers but never female flowers
rationale: Monocarpic plants have one reproductive episode before dying; the term does not mean one individual flower.

prompt: Young agave rosettes growing beside the parent are commonly propagated as what?
rationale: Agaves can form daughter rosettes called offsets, which can be separated for propagation.
